items.summary: 11月6日起，豆包工作个人版取消5小时额度限制。调整后，个人用户不再受到5小时短周期额度限制，可以在周额度范围内，根据实际工作节奏灵活安排使用时间。周额度及其他使用规则仍以对应套餐为准。 据了解，此前豆包工作个人版与市面上主流大模型类似，采用5小时、7天双周期额度管理。即使周额度仍有剩余，用户在达到5小时额度上限后，也需等待短周期额度重置才能继续使用。 此次豆包工作取消5小时额度限制后，个人用户可以更自由地分配一周内的使用额度。比如，在项目汇报前集中梳理资料、准备方案和修改演示文稿；在求职或述职阶段连续完成信息整理、内容撰写和多轮调整；也可以一次性处理较长的研究、分析与创作任务，不必因为达到短周期上限暂停工作。用户也可在豆包工作个人版“设置-订阅与额度管理”中进一步查看当前套餐、剩余额度及具体使用规则。 雷峰网 雷峰网

items.summary: 物理智能的核心挑战：让 AI 在充满不确定性、行动后果难以撤销的真实世界中，形成感知、预测、行动与持续学习的完整闭环。 作者丨张 驰 编辑丨马晓宁 大语言模型已经得到了长足的发展，但 AI 的许多能力仍然发生在屏幕之内：理解文字、生成内容、编写代码，以及调用数字工具。把这些能力带入工厂、实验室和城市设施，意味着智能系统必须进一步面对物体、空间、力与时间，在持续变化的环境中作出判断，并承担行动的实际后果。 AI 如何从处理数字信息走向可靠地参与物理过程，正是 “ 物 理智能 ” 要回答的问题。 这一步跨越的难度，很难仅用模型参数或推理能力来衡量。机器人拿起一只杯子，既要识别位置和形状，也要判断接触、摩擦与受力；实验设备执行一次操作，既要理解任务，还要满足精度、时延和安全约束。 网页操作失误可以刷新，物理世界中的碰撞、损坏却未必能够撤销。感知是否及时、动作是否可控、失败后能否恢复，都会直接影响

items.summary: “We do not sell products. We build experiences.” If that sounds like a chatbot, there’s a name for it. A new preprint examines why AI models use epanorthosis, a self-correcting figure from classical rhetoric.

items.title: Why humans punish: A study of two distinct societies reveals a shared sense of justice
items.summary: Research across two vastly different cultures reveals that our urge to punish rule-breakers balances a dual desire: to compensate victims for their exact losses and to impose extra penalties that deter future harms.

items.title: Brain stimulation made people see sexualized women less like objects in a lab test
items.summary: Is seeing women as objects a fixed feature of perception? A new brain stimulation study suggests it may be more like a habit, one that a mild electrical current can shift, at least in the lab.

items.title: The science behind the sports betting harm spiral
items.summary: Frequent sports betting increases gambling harm by making bettors highly competitive and overly confident. When financial losses accumulate, gamblers are more likely to seek professional support if they blame bad luck rather than their own poor judgment.

items.title: People high in narcissism show less coordinated brain responses to others’ embarrassment
items.summary: People low in narcissism show closely matched brain activity when watching someone else get harshly criticized. Among people high in grandiose narcissism, a new study finds, those responses are more out of sync.

items.title: Unpredictable home lives are linked to children’s mental health problems, beyond abuse and neglect
items.summary: Standard screens for childhood adversity ask about abuse, neglect and household dysfunction. A study of nearly 30,000 children found that also asking about unpredictability at home identified some kids at risk for depression whom the standard screen missed.

items.title: A bad day at work may leave you feeling less in love, study suggests
items.summary: Work deadlines, family arguments, and car trouble may not stay outside the relationship. A two-week diary study suggests that when outside hassles pile up beyond the usual, feelings of love and passion tend to dip that day.

items.title: Transgender women show distinct patterns of resting brain activity, small study finds
items.summary: A small brain imaging study found that transgender women differed from both cisgender men and women in brain networks that handle bodily sensations and movement. On most measures, cisgender men fell between the two other groups.

items.title: In strained families, extraverted parents are more likely to be cut off by their adult children
items.summary: Enthusiastic, outgoing parents may be more likely to be cut off by adult children in tense relationships, possibly because their bids for frequent contact feel overwhelming, the researchers suggest.

items.title: A 1972 school law had an unexpected effect on dementia 50 years later
items.summary: Staying in school one extra year as a teenager appears to lower the chances of a dementia diagnosis later in life, and the benefit seemed strongest among people genetically predisposed to the disease.

items.title: New neuroscience research reveals a common brain pattern across many psychiatric diagnoses
items.summary: When people shift from rest to a demanding task, their brain networks reorganize. A new study suggests this reorganization is flatter in people with psychiatric diagnoses, across conditions from depression to schizophrenia.

items.title: Psychologists petition to create a psychedelic science division within the APA
items.summary: A group of psychologists has launched a petition to create a Division of Psychedelic Science and Practice within the American Psychological Association, arguing the field is now an enduring area of psychological inquiry.

items.title: Loving-kindness meditation fails to beat muscle relaxation for pain or social well-being in online trial
items.summary: Loving-kindness meditation is meant to foster warmth toward others, but in a four-week online trial, it did not boost social support or ease pain any more than a simple muscle relaxation routine.

items.title: Losing childhood weight by adulthood might erase later depression risks
items.summary: A massive new study shows that while being heavier or thinner than average in childhood is linked to mental health risks, reaching a normal weight by adulthood might erase that excess vulnerability to depression and anxiety.

items.title: Women don’t find deeper-than-average voices more attractive when they can see the man
items.summary: When people could see a man’s full body on video, digitally deepening his voice made him seem stronger and more dominant, but not more attractive to women, a study in Royal Society Open Science found.

items.title: Voters value long-term economic growth more than previously thought, study finds
items.summary: New research reveals that voters are not simply shortsighted when evaluating the economy. Instead of focusing only on the immediate past, people consistently prefer a steady upward trajectory, even if it means sacrificing overall benefits.

items.title: Scientists map a blood protein fingerprint of menopause tied to brain health
items.summary: Blood proteins tied to inflammation, nerve cell connections, and Alzheimer’s biology shift across menopause, and older women with more of this pattern tend to show faster cognitive decline, a multi-cohort study suggests.

items.title: Social anxiety might not warp how we perceive eye contact
items.summary: A new study challenges the idea that people with social anxiety consistently perceive strangers as staring at them. Fresh experiments show that the link between anxiety and warped gaze perception is weak and difficult to replicate.

items.title: In female mice modeling schizophrenia, a single dose of psilocybin restored sensory filtering for days
items.summary: People with schizophrenia are usually excluded from psychedelic trials. A new mouse study suggests the picture is complicated: psilocybin amplified immediate reactions in a schizophrenia model but lastingly improved sensory filtering in females.

items.title: Could psychedelics aid therapy for personality disorders? An unusual case offers a first look
items.summary: A 37-year-old woman with severe personality disorders took psychedelics on her own during a year of therapy, despite her clinicians’ concerns. By the end, she no longer met criteria for two of her four diagnoses.

items.title: Scientists may have finally explained why our brains and bodies are cross-wired
items.summary: Scientists propose that the brain’s mysterious cross-wiring, which connects each hemisphere to the opposite side of the body, may have originated more than 500 million years ago in the visual systems of ancient fish. Rather than evolving for a specific advantage, this unusual arrangement may simply be a legacy of evolution building new brain circuits on an ancient foundation.

items.title: Scientists identify two overlooked skills that predict reading success
items.summary: A massive new study reveals that intelligence plays a surprisingly limited role in children's reading success, while visual processing showed no meaningful connection at all. Instead, the strongest predictors are sound recognition, vocabulary, and background knowledge, offering new clues about how to help struggling readers.

items.title: The brain’s hidden fear mechanism may explain anxiety and PTSD
items.summary: A surprising new discovery suggests that fear may cause the brain to blur the line between danger and safety rather than distinguish them more clearly. By observing brain activity in mice using augmented reality, scientists found that memories of threatening and harmless environments began to overlap, potentially allowing faster responses to danger. This "better safe than sorry" survival mechanism

items.title: Scientists discover mysterious “lonely” brain waves linked to memory loss
items.summary: Scientists have uncovered a surprising link between Alzheimer’s-related protein buildup, disrupted brain waves during deep sleep, and fading memory. The findings suggest that hidden changes in how the brain processes memories overnight may contribute to age-related memory loss long before Alzheimer’s symptoms appear.

items.title: Scientists discover a surprising brain benefit of eating peanuts every day
items.summary: A surprising new study suggests that eating peanuts every day could help support brain health and memory in older adults. Researchers found that consuming about two servings of unsalted, skin-roasted peanuts daily for 16 weeks improved insulin responsiveness in brain regions important for memory, a function that often weakens with age and has been linked to Alzheimer's disease.

items.title: Scientists discover why chronic back pain feels so personal
items.summary: A surprising discovery at UC San Diego suggests that chronic lower back pain may become deeply embedded in the brain's sense of personal identity. Researchers found that movement-triggered pain activates a brain network associated with self-awareness and memories, even though ordinary acute pain typically shuts this network down. This unexpected difference could explain why conventional pain medic

items.title: The autistic brain processes faces differently than scientists thought
items.summary: A major new study reveals that autistic children’s brains process faces differently, and those differences may begin earlier than scientists previously thought. Researchers found that brain signals associated with recognizing faces become more specialized as neurotypical children grow older, but show much less change in autistic children. The discovery could help explain why some autistic people h

items.title: This mysterious mushroom makes people see hundreds of tiny humans
items.summary: For nearly a century, people in distant parts of the world have reported a bizarre experience after eating certain wild mushrooms: seeing dozens or even hundreds of tiny, colorful humans moving through the real world. Now, scientists have identified a mushroom species, Lanmaoa asiatica, responsible for these extraordinary hallucinations in China and the Philippines.

items.title: Mediterranean diet may boost tiny proteins that protect the heart and brain
items.summary: Scientists have uncovered a surprising new clue to why the Mediterranean diet is so good for the heart, brain, and healthy aging. Researchers at USC found that older adults who closely followed the diet had higher levels of two tiny proteins, humanin and SHMOOSE, produced by the mitochondria, the energy-producing structures inside cells. These proteins have been linked to protection against heart

items.title: Breakthrough PTSD treatment achieves 68% remission rate in clinical trial
items.summary: A newly FDA-cleared PTSD treatment uses personalized brain mapping and magnetic stimulation to target abnormal brain activity, with a clinical trial reporting a 52% reduction in symptoms and 68% remission. Researchers believe the technology could transform PTSD care and pave the way for more precise treatments for other mental health conditions.

items.title: Scientists discover a hidden messaging system deep inside the brain
items.summary: A tiny region deep within the brain has surprised scientists by revealing a remarkably sophisticated communication system. Previously thought to broadcast the same chemical signal throughout the brain, this region actually sends targeted messages that help control learning, attention, and behavior, according to new research in mice.

items.title: Scientists discover a surprising secret behind the human brain’s wrinkles
items.summary: Scientists have discovered why common marmosets have unusually small, smooth brains despite starting development much like other primates. The secret lies in subtle changes to brain-building cells that slow neuron production, revealing new clues about how the large, folded human brain evolved.

items.title: Millions take fish oil for brain health. A two-year study found no benefit
items.summary: A surprising two-year clinical trial found that fish oil supplements successfully delivered omega-3s to the brain but failed to improve memory or protect against Alzheimer's-related brain shrinkage. Researchers suspect that getting these nutrients through a healthy diet may offer benefits that supplements alone cannot provide.

items.title: Your aging brain may be trading memory for something more valuable
items.summary: The aging brain may be undergoing a remarkable transformation rather than simply losing its abilities, shifting its focus from remembering details to understanding the bigger picture. Scientists suggest this change could be an evolutionary adaptation that helps older adults develop wisdom and share decades of knowledge with younger generations.

items.title: Why some people escape Alzheimer’s despite carrying a high-risk gene
items.summary: Scientists have discovered why some people with a high genetic risk of Alzheimer’s remain mentally sharp into their 80s, uncovering a rare mutation that protects the brain from harmful protein buildup. The findings reveal a potential new way to prevent early brain damage and could pave the way for treatments that mimic this natural defense.

items.title: "Mind-blowing" Alzheimer’s breakthrough: Two hours of sleep restored without clearing brain plaques
items.summary: Scientists have uncovered an unexpected culprit behind sleep loss in Alzheimer’s disease: overactive immune cells in the brain. By temporarily removing these cells, researchers restored more than two hours of sleep per day in mice, revealing a promising new target for treatment.

items.title: Modern neuroscience is rediscovering a surprising idea freud had 130 years ago
items.summary: Researchers have identified striking parallels between Sigmund Freud’s century-old theories and modern neuroscience, suggesting that the brain’s constant predictions shape how we experience reality. The findings could help explain why harmful thought patterns are so difficult to break and offer new insights into treating mental disorders.

items.title: Magic mushroom ingredient takes the fight out of aggressive fish
items.summary: A psychedelic compound found in magic mushrooms appears to have an unexpected effect: calming highly aggressive fish. Researchers discovered that low doses of psilocybin significantly reduced aggressive attacks in mangrove rivulus fish without disrupting their normal social interactions. The findings suggest psilocybin may selectively calm escalating aggression rather than simply suppressing all b

items.title: Scientists discover a natural compound that could protect the brain from too much salt
items.summary: Eating too much salt may do more than raise blood pressure. It could also harm memory and social behavior. In a new study, Japanese researchers discovered that a soy-derived compound called LPC70 helped protect mice from several damaging effects of a high-salt diet. Mice given the supplement had lower blood pressure, better memory, and improved social interactions compared with mice consuming exce

items.title: Scientists uncover 3 key brain pathways linked to lasting depression relief
items.summary: Researchers have uncovered three brain pathways linked to lasting improvements in people receiving deep brain stimulation for severe, treatment-resistant depression. They also discovered that patients who failed to improve after two years shared a striking pattern: insufficient stimulation of a crucial brain connection. The findings suggest that millimeters in electrode placement could make a majo

items.title: Scientists discover how deep sleep builds muscle, burns fat, and boosts the brain
items.summary: Scientists have discovered a surprising two-way relationship between sleep and growth hormone, revealing how the brain carefully balances physical recovery with wakefulness. The findings could help explain why poor sleep harms metabolism and brain health, potentially opening the door to new treatments for sleep and neurological disorders.

items.title: Mysterious brain activity under anesthesia challenges what we know about consciousness
items.summary: Even under general anesthesia, the human brain can analyze language, recognize different types of words, and predict what comes next in a story, according to a surprising discovery by Baylor researchers. The findings challenge our understanding of consciousness and suggest that the unconscious brain is far more capable than scientists previously realized.

items.title: Yale scientists discover how stress changes the brain to make memories stronger
items.summary: Yale scientists have uncovered how the stress hormone cortisol helps the brain turn emotional experiences into stronger, longer-lasting memories. The discovery reveals that stress can reshape communication between brain networks involved in emotion and memory, potentially explaining why certain moments are so difficult to forget.

items.title: The secret to handling stress better may start at breakfast
items.summary: Your daily routine could have a bigger impact on your ability to handle stress than you realize. A Binghamton University study of approximately 400 college students found that eating breakfast regularly, exercising, sleeping well, and taking fish oil were associated with greater psychological flexibility, which helps people adapt to stressful situations. items.title: Scientists uncover a hidden map of the brain with 539 distinct regions
items.summary: Scientists have uncovered a hidden layer of organization in the brain by creating the first detailed 3D map of its lipids, the fatty molecules essential for brain structure and communication. By analyzing millions of measurements from mouse brains, researchers identified 539 distinct chemical zones, revealing patterns and boundaries that traditional brain maps have missed. Surprisingly, even white

items.title: Scientists find hidden driver of aging and a simple amino acid that fights memory loss in mice
items.summary: Scientists discovered that declining levels of a protein called Menin may help drive aging, and restoring it in older mice reversed several age-related changes in just 30 days. Even more surprisingly, supplementing with a simple amino acid called D-serine improved memory and learning, offering a potential new approach to age-related cognitive decline.

items.title: Just 10 minutes of daily exercise could unlock deeper sleep
items.summary: Getting better sleep might be as simple as moving a little more every day. Researchers at The University of Texas at Austin found that people who exercised more frequently experienced more deep, restorative sleep, which is essential for brain recovery, memory, and emotional well-being. Surprisingly, just 10 minutes of moderate to vigorous exercise per day was associated with measurable benefits, w

items.title: Scientists discover 5 hidden brain patterns behind depression
items.summary: Depression may not be one biological condition, but several distinct patterns of brain activity hiding under the same diagnosis. Researchers studying 263 people with depression identified five brain profiles, each showing different patterns of communication between brain regions and associations with symptoms such as anxiety, trauma, and substance abuse.

items.title: After 30 years, scientists finally have a drug for a deadly brain disease
items.summary: The FDA has approved the first drug that directly targets Alexander disease, a devastating neurological disorder affecting fewer than one in a million people. Developed through decades of research, Zanvastro showed promising results in clinical trials, stabilizing motor function and even improving movement in some patients.

items.title: Loneliness may steal nearly 6 years of good health
items.summary: A large study suggests loneliness and social isolation can cost people years of healthy life, especially when it comes to mental health. Men experiencing both lost about 5.8 years free from depression and anxiety, while women lost roughly 3.7 years.

items.title: Drug target could block brain inflammation linked to Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s
items.summary: Blocking a receptor called P2X7 significantly reduced inflammation in human brain tissue, revealing a potential new treatment strategy for neurological and psychiatric disorders. The discovery could help researchers repurpose existing drugs for conditions including traumatic brain injury, Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, depression, and schizophrenia.

items.title: What happens in the brain when cannabis makes you anxious?
items.summary: Cannabinoids may intensify anxiety by removing a natural brake on specific neurons in the brain’s fear center, particularly during stressful situations. In mice, shutting down those neurons sharply reduced cannabinoid-related anxious behavior.

items.title: Vagus Nerve Stimulation Could Help New Skills Stick
items.summary: Stimulating the vagus nerve after practice helped mice develop stronger long-term motor learning, revealing a potentially important window when the brain is still locking in a new skill. The effect was linked to rhythmic changes in brain blood vessels, hinting that body-to-brain signals may help prepare the brain for lasting change.

items.title: This diet may slow brain aging by 2.5 years
items.summary: People who followed the MIND diet more closely showed slower brain shrinkage and less grey matter loss over time, with the strongest differences equivalent to about 2.5 years of delayed brain aging. Berries and poultry were linked with healthier brain changes, while sweets and fried fast foods were associated with greater tissue loss.

items.title: Could quitting ultra-processed food boost your mental health?
items.summary: People with depression who dramatically cut ultra-processed foods experienced notable improvements in their symptoms in a small preliminary study. Researchers suspect healthier eating may benefit the brain partly by reducing gut damage and chronic inflammation.

items.title: Brain scans reveal which disorders are linked to faster brain aging
items.summary: A massive MRI study found that Alzheimer’s disease, mild cognitive impairment, psychiatric disorders, and addiction are associated with distinct patterns of accelerated brain aging. The strongest effects appeared in Alzheimer’s and mild cognitive impairment, while ADHD and autism showed no significant overall difference.

items.title: Children at risk for depression get “stuck” on sad faces
items.summary: Depression may change which emotional faces children notice most, but the pattern appears to depend on family history. Children at higher familial risk became increasingly focused on sad faces, while lower-risk children with rising symptoms paid less attention to happy ones.

items.title: Scientists just discovered what coffee really does to your gut and brain
items.summary: A new study suggests coffee may influence mood and brain function by changing the activity of microbes in the gut. Both caffeinated and decaf coffee were linked to lower stress, depression, and impulsivity, while also producing measurable changes in gut bacteria and metabolites. items.title: When what you see doesn’t make sense, your brain does something remarkable
items.summary: The brain may have a built-in way to quickly settle disagreements between regions processing the same scene. Researchers found that matching signals between two visual areas lasted longer, while conflicting signals rapidly faded away. This “consensus building” mechanism could help explain how the brain turns many specialized inputs into one unified view of the world.

items.title: Coffee doesn’t have to keep you awake to disrupt your sleep
items.summary: Caffeine may make sleep less restorative even when you fall asleep normally and stay in bed for eight hours, with EEG recordings revealing fewer of the slow brain waves associated with deep sleep. Individual sensitivity varies dramatically, meaning even caffeine consumed earlier in the day could affect nighttime recovery for some people.

items.title: Scientists create a needle-thin brain implant that can do three jobs at once
items.summary: A new needle-thin brain implant can record neural activity, deliver drugs, and stimulate multiple brain regions using a single flexible fiber. Successful tests in mice suggest it could give scientists a more precise, less invasive way to study the brain and may eventually help treat neurological disorders such as epilepsy.

items.title: Scientists restore a brain protein and reverse signs of aging in mice
items.summary: Scientists found that declining levels of the brain protein Menin may help drive aging, with lower levels in mice linked to inflammation, cognitive decline, weaker bones, and thinner skin. Restoring Menin reversed several age-related changes, while the amino acid D-serine improved cognition, hinting at a potentially intriguing new target for healthy aging.

items.title: Hidden brain wiring may help keep the mind sharp as gray matter shrinks
items.summary: Scientists have discovered that the brain’s short-range wiring may help protect cognition even as gray matter shrinks with age. Healthier connections just beneath the brain’s surface were linked to better language skills and appeared to weaken the impact of gray matter loss.

items.title: Scientists find a new layer of Alzheimer’s hidden in the genome
items.summary: Scientists found that the 3D organization of DNA is disrupted in several types of brain cells affected by Alzheimer’s disease, altering how important genes are switched on and off. The discovery reveals a previously underexplored layer of the disease that could open new paths for understanding and eventually treating Alzheimer’s.

items.title: A longer exhale may push your brain toward bolder decisions
items.summary: Slow breathing with a prolonged exhale made people more willing to take risks by changing heart activity and increasing the brain’s sensitivity to rewards. The findings suggest that something as simple as controlling your breath can directly influence how you evaluate choices.

items.title: Scientists reveal the hidden instructions that build the human brain
items.summary: UCLA researchers have discovered two powerful influences that help guide how the human brain forms before birth. Radial glia, stem cells responsible for producing much of the cerebral cortex, change their behavior depending on how they process glucose and on physical contact with signals arriving from the thalamus. items.title: HEPA air purifiers may boost brain function after just one month
items.summary: Adults aged 40 and older performed about 12% faster on a test of executive function after using a HEPA air purifier at home for one month. The findings suggest that cleaner indoor air could offer a simple way to help protect the brain from the effects of traffic-related pollution.

items.title: Scientists challenge a 70-year-old “lizard brain” myth
items.summary: A long-standing picture of brain evolution as newer, rational layers stacked on top of an ancient “lizard brain” may be deeply misleading. Researchers found that evolution instead appears to balance two competing styles of brain wiring, expanding one while shrinking the other depending on what an animal needs to survive.

items.title: Too much or too little sleep may make your body age faster
items.summary: Both too little and too much sleep may be linked to faster aging throughout the body. Researchers analyzing 23 biological aging clocks found the lowest aging levels among people sleeping about 6.4 to 7.8 hours per day. Short or long sleep was also associated with numerous conditions affecting the brain, heart, lungs, metabolism, and digestive system.

items.title: Childhood trauma may leave a lasting “scar” inside brain cells
items.summary: Early-life stress may physically alter how DNA is packaged in the brain, leaving stress-related genes primed to activate more easily years later. In mice, researchers were able to block this effect, preventing the heightened anxiety and stress sensitivity that otherwise appeared in adulthood.

items.title: Your brain may not actually “make” decisions
items.summary: A neuroscientist is challenging the idea that the brain contains a central system that actually “makes” our decisions. What we experience as choosing may instead emerge from the continuous interaction of perception, movement, the body, and the world around us.

items.title: Depression may shut down the brain’s ability to make new neurons
items.summary: A major study found that adults with depression show disrupted production of new neurons in the hippocampus, potentially weakening the brain’s ability to separate new experiences from painful memories. The researchers also identified broad molecular changes that could open the door to new treatments tailored to different biological forms of depression.

items.title: A major Alzheimer’s risk gene may shrink brain cells years before symptoms
items.summary: Researchers have uncovered a possible reason why the Alzheimer’s risk gene APOE4 can disrupt the brain long before memory problems begin. In mice, APOE4 increased a protein called Nell2, shrinking neurons and making memory circuits unusually active. That early hyperactivity predicted worse memory later in life. items.title: Schizophrenia’s lost brain connections follow a surprising pattern
items.summary: Specialized brain scans reveal that schizophrenia is linked to widespread loss of the synapses that connect brain cells, with the left side of the brain hit especially hard. The damage follows a surprisingly organized pattern tied to the brain’s chemistry and wiring. Researchers also identified a left frontal region that may serve as a starting point for the loss.

items.title: Scientists reveal how the brain changes its connections when uncertainty strikes
items.summary: The brain has a remarkably flexible system for handling uncertainty and changing situations. Researchers found that the frontoparietal cortex constantly shifts how it communicates with other brain regions depending on what information is needed to make a decision. Rather than simply becoming more active when things get difficult, this network appears to reorganize itself in real time.

items.title: A therapy that “rewrites” childhood memories can ease fear of failure
items.summary: Childhood criticism can leave people carrying a fear of failure long into adulthood, but new research suggests those emotional patterns may be surprisingly flexible. Young adults who revisited painful memories through imagery-based therapy showed lasting reductions in fear, guilt, sadness, and stress.

items.title: A little-known protein may be fueling Alzheimer’s — and scientists found a way to block it
items.summary: An experimental Alzheimer’s compound prevented damaging protein clumps from forming in the brains of mice, helping nerve cells survive longer and reducing amyloid buildup. The treatment also appeared to improve heart health and slow some signs of aging, raising hopes for an entirely new way to combat dementia.

items.title: A stress hormone may help the brain repair itself
items.summary: A surprising stress-related signal may help the brain repair itself after injury. Researchers found that myelin-producing precursor cells rapidly release the stress hormone CRH near damaged brain tissue, helping control how those cells mature and rebuild protective nerve insulation. items.title: Scientists discover a hidden brain rhythm that could improve Parkinson’s treatment
items.summary: Scientists have pinpointed a brain network—and its distinctive electrical rhythm—that appears to drive the benefits of deep brain stimulation for Parkinson’s disease. The discovery could lead to more precise, personalized stimulation settings and better results for patients.

items.title: Ozempic may have revealed the brain’s hidden “craving center”
items.summary: Ozempic-like drugs appear to weaken more than hunger—they may also reduce cravings for alcohol and other addictive substances. Scientists are increasingly tracing this effect to the lateral septum, a brain region that helps connect memories and surroundings with rewarding experiences. items.summary: Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 26 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02620-3 People will often trust or distrust an artificial intelligence (AI) output because of how it makes them feel, rather than how reliable it is. items.title: Decredentialed jobs and upward mobility among non-college workers in the USA
items.summary: Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 26 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02610-5 Linking job postings to US Census earnings records from 2011 to 2021, Lyttelton et al. find that non-college workers hired into jobs that dropped degree requirements earned around US$4,600 more per year, yet employers rarely hired non-college workers after decredentialing.

items.title: Within-family heritability estimates for behavioural and disease phenotypes from 500,000 sibling pairs of diverse ancestries
items.summary: Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 26 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02599-x Using the variation in DNA sharing between 500,000 sibling pairs with diverse genetic ancestries, Yengo et al. estimate the heritability of 14 complex traits.

items.title: Generative AI and the temporary upskilling of knowledge workers
items.summary: Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 26 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02566-6 This randomized trial by Wiles et al. shows that generative AI helps knowledge workers perform data science tasks outside their skill set, but workers do not retain the underlying knowledge when the tool is removed.

items.title: Turing-like tests for language and vision demonstrate a narrowing gap between humans and AI
items.summary: Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 26 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02590-6 Zhang et al. systematically compare humans and AI across three language and three vision tasks.

items.title: Large language models for computational social science
